subject: checks-and-balances
title: Checks and Balances: Designing Against Power
summary: How the Constitution sets the branches against each other, and the debate about it.

keys.prompt: What did Federalist No. 51 mean by "ambition must be made to counteract ambition"?
keys.answer: Don't rely on leaders being good; give each branch the tools and reasons to resist the others.

keys.prompt: Where does the courts' power to strike down laws come from?
keys.answer: It isn't spelled out in the Constitution; it was confirmed in Marbury v. Madison in 1803.

keys.prompt: What's the core debate about checks and balances?
keys.answer: Supporters say they prevent abuse and force compromise; critics say they cause gridlock. Both agree they make big change hard.

cards.title: "If men were angels…"
cards.text: In Federalist No. 51, the case for the Constitution was put bluntly: "If men were angels, no government would be necessary." So if people aren't angels, how do you design a government that controls itself?

cards.question: "If men were angels, no government would be necessary." So how did the Constitution's designers plan to keep government in check?

options.text: Trust leaders to be good people
Give each branch tools and reasons to resist the others
Let one branch supervise all the others

cards.reveal: Instead of trusting leaders to be good, they set "ambition" against "ambition": each branch gets tools and reasons to resist the others.

cards.title: Ambition vs. ambition
cards.text: The same essay says "Ambition must be made to counteract ambition." Instead of trusting leaders to be good, the design gives each branch tools and reasons to resist the others.

cards.title: Veto and override
cards.text: The President can veto a bill. Congress can override it, but only if two thirds of the House and two thirds of the Senate agree. The Senate also must give "advice and consent" before the President can appoint judges.

cards.title: Impeachment and judicial review
cards.text: The House can impeach, which means formally accuse, an official. The Senate holds the trial, and it takes two thirds of senators present to convict. Courts can strike down unconstitutional laws. That power is not spelled out in the Constitution. It was confirmed in 1803 in Marbury v. Madison.

cards.title: The debate
cards.text: Supporters say checks and balances prevent abuse and force compromise. Critics say they can cause gridlock, so government responds slowly when problems need action. Both sides agree the system makes big changes hard. They disagree about whether that is a feature or a bug.

why.q: Two people can agree on the facts about gridlock and still disagree about the system. Why?
why.a: Both agree it makes big changes hard. They disagree about whether that is a feature (fewer mistakes) or a bug (slower fixes).

cards.question: Is it better for a system to make change hard (to prevent mistakes) or easy (to fix problems fast)? Does your answer depend on who is in charge?
nudges: Try arguing the side you don't agree with.
Think of a school, team, or company rule. Who can overrule whom?

questions.q: What does it take to override a presidential veto?

options.text: Two thirds of both the House and the Senate
options.why: Right. It is a high bar on purpose.

options.text: A simple majority of the Senate
options.why: A majority passes a bill. Overriding a veto takes two thirds of each house.
Courts don't override vetoes. Congress does.

questions.q: Where does the courts' power to strike down unconstitutional laws come from?

options.text: It was confirmed in Marbury v. Madison (1803); it is not spelled out in the Constitution.
options.why: Right. The Supreme Court itself notes it is not explicit in the text.

options.text: Article I lists it word for word.
options.why: The Court notes judicial review is not explicitly provided in the Constitution.

questions.q: Which statement fairly describes the debate about checks and balances?

options.text: Supporters stress preventing abuse; critics stress gridlock and slow responses.
options.why: Yes. Both describe real effects; people weigh them differently.

options.text: Everyone agrees they only have benefits.
options.why: There is a real debate about the costs.

options.text: Only one political party supports them.
options.why: Support and criticism come from many viewpoints.

sources.supports: Veto override by two thirds of each House; the President shall "take Care that the Laws be faithfully executed"; Senate advice and consent for judges; House impeaches, Senate tries, two-thirds to convict, judgment limited to removal and disqualification.

sources.supports: Federalist No. 51: "If men were angels, no government would be necessary" and "Ambition must be made to counteract ambition."
